Restricted push: fold every unallowed project into one per-account bucket, no pseudonyms
description:
Today a restricted machine sends each unallowed project under its own salted pseudonym (src/ccreport/push.py:248 `redact`), and the server draws a row per pseudonym with real cost and tokens. The dashboard therefore shows how many private projects exist and what each one costs. That is the leak: the count and the shape of the work.

Wanted: the server renders no unallowed project at all. Every unallowed record folds into ONE bucket per account, named from the account.

Client side (src/ccreport/push.py):
- `redact` sets project=None, sid=None, cwd=None, repo=None for a record whose project is not in `allow`. No per-project pseudonym, no per-session pseudonym.
- `pseudonym` and `pseudo_session` (push.py:227, :238) lose their only caller. The `salt` field in push.toml and the salt written by `ccreport server connect` become dead — decide in the change whether to keep writing it (harmless, and re-adding a pseudonym later needs it) or drop it from the config and from ServerConfig.
- `policy_hash` (push.py:268) must move when this ships, or every already-pushed file keeps its pseudonym rows: the material it hashes is unchanged by a code edit. Add a redaction-shape constant to that material and bump it. Ingest replaces a file's rows wholesale, and a policy change already sets `replace` on every file, so the old pseudonym rows disappear as the re-push walks the corpus. No server-side purge is needed.

Server side (src/ccreport/server/reports.py):
- A record with project NULL renders as the bucket name instead of NULL. Both builders spell the project the same way today — reports.py:116 (full record path) and reports.py:213 (grouped path) — so the fold belongs there, beside the account resolution.
- Assumed name: `<account display>/aggregated`, where the account display is the alias from ccreport-1fz1 when one is set, and the account label or uuid otherwise. So `post@rykroken.net/aggregated` before an alias and `personal/aggregated` after. The other reading of the request — `<account-id>/<alias>-aggregated`, keeping both — is one f-string away if that is what was meant.
- The bucket must group: two unallowed projects on the same account are one row, one project entry in the dashboard breakdown and one entry in `ccreport --server URL project`.
- The server holds no policy, so it cannot tell a NULL project from a restricted machine apart from a NULL from anything else. NULL only ever arrives from redaction today; if that stops being true the bucket needs a marker column instead.

Depends on ccreport-1fz1 for the alias half of the name; ships without it by falling back to account_label.
acceptance:
- A restricted machine's unallowed projects arrive with project, sid, cwd and repo all NULL, and no salted value anywhere in the request.
- The dashboard's project breakdown shows exactly one row per account for all unallowed spend, and the cost and token totals are unchanged from today.
- That row is named `<account label>/aggregated` while the account has no alias, and `<alias>-aggregated` once it has one. `post@rykroken.net/personal-aggregated` is never rendered.
- An account whose records carry no label falls back to `<account uuid>/aggregated`.
- `ccreport --server URL project` shows the same single row under the same name.
- Setting or clearing an account alias renames the bucket on the next render, with no push and no restart.
- Shipping the change forces a full re-push (a redaction-shape constant moves policy_hash), and after it no pseudonym row remains on the server.
- The salt is still written by `ccreport server connect` and still in the policy_hash material, with no caller.
- An allowed project is untouched: real name, real cwd, real repo, real session id.
- tests/test_push_policy.py covers the fold and the policy_hash move; tests/test_server_reports.py and tests/test_dashboard.py cover both name forms, the uuid fallback, the grouping and the alias rename; `just lint-all` and `just test` pass.
notes:
DECIDED — bucket name (supersedes the assumed name in the description):

  alias set      ->  `<alias>-aggregated`        e.g. `personal-aggregated`
  no alias       ->  `<account label>/aggregated` e.g. `post@rykroken.net/aggregated`

The email appears only while nothing better exists. Setting an alias removes it
from the string entirely, so `post@rykroken.net/personal-aggregated` must never
be rendered — the alias replaces the whole account segment, slash included.
Fall back to the account uuid where a record carries no label.

One row per account in the project breakdown either way.

DECIDED — salt: keep it. `ccreport server connect` still generates and writes
it, `ServerConfig.salt` stays, and it stays in the policy_hash material, with no
caller once `redact` stops pseudonymizing. `pseudonym` and `pseudo_session`
stay in push.py unused, so re-introducing a pseudonym later needs no config
migration. Because the salt no longer changes when the redaction shape does, the
redaction-shape constant in the policy_hash material is what forces the
re-push — it is not optional.

Sessions are not exempt: sid goes to NULL with project, cwd and repo. A session
count per bucket is itself a signal about the hidden work.

Restricted push: fold every unallowed project into one per-account bucket, no pseudonyms
description:
Today a restricted machine sends each unallowed project under its own salted pseudonym (src/ccreport/push.py:248 `redact`), and the server draws a row per pseudonym with real cost and tokens. The dashboard therefore shows how many private projects exist and what each one costs. That is the leak: the count and the shape of the work.

Wanted: the server renders no unallowed project at all. Every unallowed record folds into ONE bucket per account, named from the account.

Client side (src/ccreport/push.py):
- `redact` sets project=None, sid=None, cwd=None, repo=None for a record whose project is not in `allow`. No per-project pseudonym, no per-session pseudonym.
- `pseudonym` and `pseudo_session` (push.py:227, :238) lose their only caller. The `salt` field in push.toml and the salt written by `ccreport server connect` become dead — decide in the change whether to keep writing it (harmless, and re-adding a pseudonym later needs it) or drop it from the config and from ServerConfig.
- `policy_hash` (push.py:268) must move when this ships, or every already-pushed file keeps its pseudonym rows: the material it hashes is unchanged by a code edit. Add a redaction-shape constant to that material and bump it. Ingest replaces a file's rows wholesale, and a policy change already sets `replace` on every file, so the old pseudonym rows disappear as the re-push walks the corpus. No server-side purge is needed.

Server side (src/ccreport/server/reports.py):
- A record with project NULL renders as the bucket name instead of NULL. Both builders spell the project the same way today — reports.py:116 (full record path) and reports.py:213 (grouped path) — so the fold belongs there, beside the account resolution.
- Assumed name: `<account display>/aggregated`, where the account display is the alias from ccreport-1fz1 when one is set, and the account label or uuid otherwise. So `post@rykroken.net/aggregated` before an alias and `personal/aggregated` after. The other reading of the request — `<account-id>/<alias>-aggregated`, keeping both — is one f-string away if that is what was meant.
- The bucket must group: two unallowed projects on the same account are one row, one project entry in the dashboard breakdown and one entry in `ccreport --server URL project`.
- The server holds no policy, so it cannot tell a NULL project from a restricted machine apart from a NULL from anything else. NULL only ever arrives from redaction today; if that stops being true the bucket needs a marker column instead.

Depends on ccreport-1fz1 for the alias half of the name; ships without it by falling back to account_label.
acceptance:
- A restricted machine's unallowed projects arrive with project, sid, cwd and repo all NULL, and no salted value anywhere in the request.
- The dashboard's project breakdown shows exactly one row per account for all unallowed spend, and the cost and token totals are unchanged from today.
- That row is named `<account label>/aggregated` while the account has no alias, and `<alias>-aggregated` once it has one. `post@rykroken.net/personal-aggregated` is never rendered.
- An account whose records carry no label falls back to `<account uuid>/aggregated`.
- `ccreport --server URL project` shows the same single row under the same name.
- Setting or clearing an account alias renames the bucket on the next render, with no push and no restart.
- Shipping the change forces a full re-push (a redaction-shape constant moves policy_hash), and after it no pseudonym row remains on the server.
- The salt is still written by `ccreport server connect` and still in the policy_hash material, with no caller.
- An allowed project is untouched: real name, real cwd, real repo, real session id.
- tests/test_push_policy.py covers the fold and the policy_hash move; tests/test_server_reports.py and tests/test_dashboard.py cover both name forms, the uuid fallback, the grouping and the alias rename; `just lint-all` and `just test` pass.
notes:
DECIDED — bucket name (supersedes the assumed name in the description):

  alias set      ->  `<alias>-aggregated`        e.g. `personal-aggregated`
  no alias       ->  `<account label>/aggregated` e.g. `post@rykroken.net/aggregated`

The email appears only while nothing better exists. Setting an alias removes it
from the string entirely, so `post@rykroken.net/personal-aggregated` must never
be rendered — the alias replaces the whole account segment, slash included.
Fall back to the account uuid where a record carries no label.

One row per account in the project breakdown either way.

DECIDED — salt: keep it. `ccreport server connect` still generates and writes
it, `ServerConfig.salt` stays, and it stays in the policy_hash material, with no
caller once `redact` stops pseudonymizing. `pseudonym` and `pseudo_session`
stay in push.py unused, so re-introducing a pseudonym later needs no config
migration. Because the salt no longer changes when the redaction shape does, the
redaction-shape constant in the policy_hash material is what forces the
re-push — it is not optional.

count per bucket is itself a signal about the hidden work.
closed_reason: redact nulls project, sid, cwd and repo; server folds them into one bucket per account

ccreport server allow/deny: accept several projects and infer the single server
description:
`ccreport server allow macsetup dogcat py_project_template` fails with `unrecognized arguments: py_project_template`.

Two separate limits in the parser at src/ccreport/ccreport.py:3000-3002 (the `if name in ("allow", "deny")` branch):

1. `project` is a single positional, so only one project can be allowed or denied per invocation.
2. `url` is a required positional, so the URL must be typed even when push.toml names exactly one server. In the failing command above, `macsetup` was swallowed as the URL and `dogcat` as the project.

cmd_server_allow (src/ccreport/ccreport.py:1723) already calls _resolved_projects([args.project]) — a list of one — so the resolve, the set union/difference, the write_server call and the clear_push_state call all take a list unchanged.

Proposed shape:
- Replace the two positionals with one variadic `targets` (nargs="+").
- If targets[0] is a key in push.read_raw(path), it is the URL and the rest are projects.
- Otherwise, if push.toml names exactly one server, use it and treat every target as a project.
- If targets[0] starts with http:// or https:// and is not configured, that is still the unknown-server error it is today (tests/test_push_policy.py::TestAllowDenyCommands::test_an_unknown_server_is_an_error covers it) — do not fall through to treating a URL as a project name.
- Error when no project is left after the URL is consumed, and when several servers are configured and no URL was given (name them).
- Update the two --help strings for the new positional.

Note push.toml is written by `ccreport server connect` and the allow list is read back through push.load_config.
acceptance:
- `ccreport server allow <url> a b c` adds all three to that server's allow list; `deny` removes all three.
- With exactly one server in push.toml, `ccreport server allow a b c` works without a URL.
- `ccreport server allow https://nowhere.example x` still exits 1 when that URL is not configured.
- `ccreport server allow <url>` with no project exits 1 with a message naming the gap.
- With two servers configured and no URL, the command exits 1 and prints both URLs.
- The watermark is still cleared once per run (cache_db.clear_push_state).
- New tests in tests/test_push_policy.py::TestAllowDenyCommands cover multi-project allow, multi-project deny, and URL omission; `just lint-all` and `just test` pass.
closed_reason: One variadic targets positional; the URL is inferred when push.toml names one server

Server UI: delete a token and delete a machine outright
description:
The web UI can mint and revoke, and that is all. A machine minted by mistake — http://10.172.1.236:8787/machines/aa — stays in the list forever, and a revoked token stays in its machine's table forever. Both need a delete.

What exists now:
- db.revoke_token (src/ccreport/server/db.py:263) stamps revoked_at; nothing ever removes the row. The button is in server/templates/machine.html and posts to /tokens/{token_hash}/revoke (src/ccreport/server/pages.py:132).
- machine_tokens, server_records and ingest_files all declare `REFERENCES machines(machine_id) ON DELETE CASCADE`, and db.connect sets `PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON` (db.py:214), so deleting the machines row already deletes all three. This is why the confirmation matters: a machine with records holds real money.

Decision (asked and answered): one delete removes everything — the machine, its tokens, its ingest_files and every server_record it pushed — behind typing the machine id to confirm.

Proposed shape:
- db.delete_token(conn, token_hash) -> bool, deleting the row rather than stamping it. Keep revoke: revoking is what you do to a machine that is still out there, deleting is what you do to a mistake.
- db.delete_machine(conn, machine_id) -> int, returning the record count it destroyed, letting the cascade do the rest.
- POST /tokens/{token_hash}/delete beside the existing revoke route, and a Delete button in machine.html's token table next to Revoke.
- POST /machines/{machine_id}/delete, guarded by a form field the person must type the machine id into; a mismatch re-renders the page with an error and deletes nothing. Redirect to /machines on success with a line naming what went: "Deleted aa and its 0 records."
- A machine that no longer exists is a 404 on GET /machines/{id} already (pages.py:68-79); after deletion that is the correct state.
- dashboard.cached_build keys on db.content_stamp — deleting records must move that stamp or the dashboard keeps drawing the deleted machine's spend.

Related: ccreport-1fz1 adds an Accounts tab to the same UI; the two touch pages.py and base.html but not the same routes.
acceptance:
- The token table has a Delete button; deleting removes the row entirely, and the machine's next push with that token is rejected.
- Revoke still exists and still only stamps revoked_at.
- POST /machines/{id}/delete with the typed id matching deletes the machine, its tokens, its ingest_files and its server_records, then redirects to /machines naming the record count destroyed.
- A mismatched or empty confirmation deletes nothing and re-renders with an error.
- Deleting a machine that pushed records changes db.content_stamp, so the dashboard drops its spend on the next render.
- GET /machines/{id} for the deleted machine is a 404.
- Tests in tests/test_server_pages.py cover token delete, machine delete with records, the refused confirmation and the 404; `just lint-all` and `just test` pass.
closed_reason: Token delete beside revoke; machine delete behind the typed id, cascading to records

Versioned migration runner shared by cache.db and the server database
description:
The server database has no migration path. src/ccreport/server/db.py:227 compares
PRAGMA user_version against SCHEMA_VERSION and, when they differ, runs _SCHEMA_SQL --
which is CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS throughout. On an existing server file every one
of those creates is a no-op, so a column added to server_records never appears and
bumping SCHEMA_VERSION changes nothing. The docstring at db.py:21 tells the next agent
to bump it, which reads as a working mechanism and is not one. That file is the only
copy of a machine's records once its JSONL logs have rotated, so the failure mode is a
query against a missing column on a database nothing can rebuild.

cache.db does migrate, ad hoc: _ADDED_COLUMNS (cache_db.py:379) for plain ADD COLUMN,
plus five meta-flagged steps in _run_migrations (cache_db.py:607-781). Each step
hand-rolls its own BEGIN IMMEDIATE, rollback handler and post-hoc verification, and
the flag write is what makes it once-only. It works; it is copy-pasted per step and
has no ordering, no log and no guard against an edited step.

Reference implementation studied: /Users/ove/Trash/migrate (src/migra/db/migration/).
Four things there fit ccreport:

1. A numbered chain validated at load -- gaps and duplicate versions are hard errors
   (migrations.py:361, _validate_migrations).
2. The step and its version bump applied in ONE executescript, so a crash cannot land
   between the schema change and the pointer update (migrations.py:480).
3. A migration_checksum table: refuse to start when a version that was already applied
   no longer matches the code that ran (migrations.py:432).
4. An flock file beside the database, taken for the whole run (migrations.py:144).
   ccreport needs this: statusline, push and ccu open cache.db from separate processes
   concurrently, and today two of them can enter the bootstrap at once.

Do NOT copy from it: the .sql-file format (ccreport migrations carry Python logic --
migration 2b at cache_db.py:651 matches model names by substring, which SQL cannot
express), the 1:1 testfile pairing, the symlink/BOM/filename-case hardening (that
guards an operator-supplied directory; ccreport ships its steps in its own package),
or the psqtie DB wrapper.

Shape agreed with the user: one shared module (e.g. src/ccreport/migrations.py) that
both databases call. Steps are Python callables in a numbered list, one list per
database. PRAGMA user_version stays the pointer -- both files already use it. The
existing cache_db meta flags must keep working: a database that already ran
migrated_dedup_keys_pk_order must not re-run it as step N.

Constraint from AGENTS.md: statusline.py imports nothing outside the stdlib and defers
cache_db into the functions that touch the DB. The new module is imported by cache_db,
not by statusline, and everything it does stays behind the user_version gate so a warm
render pays nothing.
acceptance:
- A shared migration runner exists, with steps declared as an ordered numbered list per
  database, and a gap or duplicate version raises at load rather than skipping a step.
- Each step and its version bump commit atomically; a crash mid-step leaves the DB on
  either the old or the new version, never between.
- An applied version whose step has since changed is detected and refuses to run
  further, naming the version.
- Concurrent processes cannot both apply the same step (file lock beside the DB file,
  with a bounded wait that raises rather than hanging).
- server/db.py routes schema changes through the runner; adding a column to
  server_records reaches an existing server database, proven by a test that opens a DB
  at the old schema, adds a step, reopens and asserts the column and the preserved rows.
- cache_db.py's five existing steps are expressed in the new list, and a DB carrying
  the old meta flags does not re-run any of them (test with a pre-seeded meta table).
- just lint-all and just test pass; every new public function has a pytest test.

acceptance:
- A shared migration runner exists, with steps declared as an ordered numbered list per
  database, and a gap or duplicate version raises at load rather than skipping a step.
- Each step and its version bump commit atomically; a crash mid-step leaves the DB on
  either the old or the new version, never between.
- An applied version whose step source or name has since changed is detected and
  refuses to run further, naming the version.
- Concurrent processes cannot both apply the same step (file lock beside the DB file,
  with a bounded wait that raises rather than hanging).
- server/db.py routes schema changes through the runner; adding a column to
  server_records reaches an existing server database, proven by a test that opens a DB
  at the old schema, adds a step, reopens and asserts the column and the preserved rows.
- cache_db.py routes schema changes through the runner above baseline 11. The frozen
  pre-baseline bootstrap still runs for a database below it, and a database carrying
  the old meta flags re-runs none of the five legacy steps (test with a pre-seeded
  meta table).
- SCHEMA_VERSION in both files is derived from the chain head, not hand-edited, and a
  test fails if either is set independently.
- just lint-all and just test pass; every new public function has a pytest test.
notes:
DESIGN (agreed with the user before implementation)

Module: src/ccreport/migrations.py. Stdlib only. Imported by cache_db.py and
server/db.py, never by statusline.py, and reached only behind the user_version gate.

    @dataclass(frozen=True)
    class Step:
        version: int
        name: str
        apply: Callable[[sqlite3.Connection], None] | None   # None = version bump only
        legacy_flag: str | None = None

    def run(conn, *, chain, baseline, db_path, applied_flags=None) -> int

Log table, created by run() in both databases before the first step:

    CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS schema_migrations (
        version    INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
        name       TEXT NOT NULL,
        applied_at REAL NOT NULL,
        source_sha TEXT
    );

Per step: BEGIN IMMEDIATE, apply(conn), insert the log row, PRAGMA user_version = N,
COMMIT. user_version is header state and is transactional, so no executescript splice
is needed to keep the bump with the DDL. The restriction that buys: a step runs inside
a transaction, where PRAGMA foreign_keys is a no-op, so a table rebuild must tolerate
FK enforcement staying on -- which the existing dedup_keys rebuild at cache_db.py:738
already does. A step that genuinely cannot is out of scope until one exists.

SCHEMA_VERSION stops being hand-edited in both files: it becomes chain[-1].version. A
change that only adds a table still needs a chain entry, with apply=None, to move the
version and so re-run _SCHEMA_SQL.

Numbering: continue from the current stamp. cache.db baseline is 11 and the server
baseline is 3. _SCHEMA_SQL, _ADDED_COLUMNS and the five meta-flagged steps in
_run_migrations are the frozen pre-baseline bootstrap and are NOT re-expressed as chain
entries -- a database below its baseline takes the legacy path and is then treated as
sitting at the baseline. New steps start at 12 (cache.db) and 4 (server). The rejected
alternative renumbered from 1 with each meta key as a legacy_flag skip-guard; it needs
a user_version-to-chain mapping, and one wrong entry re-runs a data migration against a
live cache.

Validation at load: versions strictly ascending by one from baseline + 1, no
duplicates, and a database whose user_version exceeds the head raises rather than
being silently downgraded.

Lock: <db_path>.migration-lock, opened O_CREAT|O_RDWR|O_NOFOLLOW at 0600, flock
LOCK_EX|LOCK_NB polled to a 60 s deadline, released after the last step. fcntl is
POSIX-only, matching this project's darwin/linux targets.

Drift guard: source_sha is sha256 over inspect.getsource(step.apply), recorded on apply
and compared on later opens. Unreadable source records NULL and is compared against
nothing. A recorded name that no longer matches the chain entry raises regardless.
inspect is imported on the migration path only.

Dashboard toggles are lost on refresh
description:
The breakdown tabs (model, day, project, machine) and the chart's Cost/Tokens toggle live in JS state alone, so a refresh drops back to model + cost. Only ?days= survives.

Put both in the query string: /?days=30&by=project&metric=tokens.

Files:
- src/ccreport/server/pages.py: index() takes by and metric, validates by against dashboard.DIMENSIONS and metric against cost|tokens, and passes both to the template. Neither belongs in dashboard.cached_build's key: the view already carries all four breakdowns and both chart series, so this only picks what renders visible.
- templates/dashboard.html: the range links carry by and metric; the dimension tabs become real hrefs so the page works with no JS; the table for by renders unhidden and its tab gets 'on'.
- static/dashboard.js: each toggle rewrites the URL with history.replaceState instead of reloading, so switching stays instant.
acceptance: Switching a breakdown tab or the chart metric updates the address bar, a reload lands on the same tab and series, a range switch keeps both, and an unknown or missing value falls back to model and cost.

Detail pages per breakdown entity, with charts
description:
Every breakdown row on the dashboard should open a page for that entity, scoped to the same range: /account/{key}, /model/{key}, /day/YYYY-MM-DD, /project/{key}, /machine/{key}.

Shape (decided with the user): the dashboard narrowed to one entity — headline, tiles, account bars, breakdown tables for the OTHER four dimensions — plus several charts that combine different metrics rather than one chart with a toggle:
  1. cost over time, one series per account
  2. cost over time, one series per model
  3. tokens over time by kind (input, output, cache write, cache read)
  4. calls per bucket

The day page charts by hour instead of by day, which needs reports.load (per-record timestamps) rather than load_grouped (which folds the hour away).

Notes:
- The scope matches the string the breakdown table shows, so redacted project buckets and account aliases link to a page that finds their rows.
- A scoped build must not enter dashboard.cached_build's cache: that is keyed on (db path, days) and holds the whole-server view.
- The catch-all route means /static has to be mounted before pages.router in factory.py, or the asset URLs match /{dimension}/{key} first.
- Chart palette: the current dashboard.js COLORS fail the dataviz validator on our dark surface (deutan dE 4.6 for green vs amber). The reference dark palette #3987e5,#d95926,#199e70,#c98500,#d55181,#008300 passes every check on #191c24.
acceptance: Each of the five dimensions has a detail page reachable from its breakdown row, the range toggle carries over, the day page charts hourly, an unknown dimension is a 404, an entity with no records renders an empty page rather than an error, and just lint-all and just test pass.

The /static mount is outside the network allowlist
description:
factory.py gates the routers with Depends(restrict_remote_addr_dep(...)), but app.mount('/static', StaticFiles(...)) takes no dependencies argument, so the mount is reachable from any address while every page it styles answers 403.

What leaks is app.css, dashboard.js, detail.js, palette.js and the vendored uPlot build — no records and no tokens — so this is a claim that is wrong rather than a disclosure. AGENTS.md says '/static is behind the gate with the pages it styles', which is what made it look covered.

Fix: wrap StaticFiles in an ASGI app that runs the same ip_allowed check (middleware.ip_allowed is already importable), or serve the assets from a gated route. Then a test that an outside address gets 403 for /static/app.css the way it does for /settings/machines — tests/test_server_pages.py::TestAccessControl is where the sibling cases live.
acceptance: An address outside the configured networks gets 403 for /static/app.css, an allowed one still gets 200 with the right content type, and the AGENTS.md sentence matches what the code does.

Bash-served full-line statusline cache, no Python on hits
description:
Serve a cache hit entirely from the bash wrapper, so a render costs no Python process at all.

Today every render execs python and goes through src/ccreport/statusline.py, even on the fast path: renders within FAST_TTL_S (15 s) already skip subprocess spawns and db reads by reusing the previous render's fetch results from a per-session temp file, and the wrapper bin/statusline-command_x.sh already skips the uv resolver. Prior measurement on an M-series machine, warm: ~110 ms before those two changes, ~25-30 ms after. What remains is interpreter startup and module import.

Proposal: cache the fully rendered line, with placeholders for the segments that must stay live. bin/statusline-command_x.sh serves that line on a hit and fills the placeholders itself — clock from $EPOCHSECONDS plus printf strftime, ctx% via jq from the stdin JSON. On a miss it falls through to Python as now. Estimated ~10 ms per hit.

Cost, which is why this is priority 3: a second formatting path in bash, and placeholder splicing that has to be kept in sync with the Python renderer whenever a segment's format changes. Only worth doing if ~25-30 ms still bothers us in practice. Requires bash 5 for $EPOCHSECONDS and printf %(fmt)T — /bin/bash is 3.2, so pin the shebang to the Homebrew bash — and jq on PATH.
acceptance:
- A cache hit renders with no python process spawned (verify with a process trace or a counter).
- Clock and ctx% are correct on every hit, not stale.
- Missing bash 5 or jq falls back to the Python renderer instead of erroring.
- Measured hit latency is reported in the issue before it moves to in_review.
- Tests under tests/ cover the placeholder contract between the Python renderer and the wrapper.

comments.author: post@rykroken.net
comments.text:
Measured on this machine (M-series, warm), 10 runs each:

- Current wrapper, fast-path hit: median 27.2 ms (26.8 min, 27.8 max). That is interpreter startup plus module import; the fast path itself does no spawns and no db reads.
- Prototype bash-only hit (Homebrew bash 5.3.15 startup + one jq call + printf): median 9.4 ms (7.7 min). The 481 ms max was one cold outlier.

So the saving is roughly 18 ms per render, and the issue's ~10 ms estimate for a hit is right.

Preconditions on this machine are met: jq 1.7.1 is on PATH and /opt/homebrew/bin/bash is 5.3.15 (/bin/bash is 3.2.57 as expected, so the shebang would have to be pinned).

Not started. The issue's own gate is a judgement — 'only worth doing if ~25-30 ms still bothers us in practice' — and the cost is a second formatting path in bash that has to be kept in sync with the Python renderer whenever a segment's format changes. That cost just went up: this session added two segments to the line (the burn ETA and the push spawn), which is the kind of churn a duplicate formatter drifts against.

comments.author: post@rykroken.net
comments.text: Decision (user, this session): leave open, not built. 27.2 ms is acceptable in practice, and the 18 ms is not worth a second formatting path in bash. The measurement above stands if this is revisited.

Drop the statusline fast cache on ConfigChange
description:
Claude Code fires a ConfigChange hook when a settings file changes (user, project, local, policy) or a skills file changes. The payload carries session_id, transcript_path, cwd, config_source and config_path. Docs: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/hooks#configchange

The status line caches its fetch results per session for FAST_TTL_S (15 s) in $TMPDIR/claude-statusline-<uid>-<sid>.json (statusline._fast_cache_path). Two of the cached values are read out of settings files: the sbx/!sbx badge, which walks local -> project -> user settings in statusline._render_sandbox (src/ccreport/statusline.py:1189), and the CLAUDE_CODE_STATUSLINE_* segment toggles that settings 'env' feeds. After an edit they stay stale for up to 15 s.

Wire a ConfigChange hook that deletes that file, so the next render takes the slow path and re-reads the settings. The memo file (.memo.json) is not touched: its DSP verdict comes from the claude process argv and its ~/.claude.json stamp is invalidated by that file's own mtime/size.

Model it on bin/clear-statusline-memo.sh: read stdin, jq the session_id, sanitize it the same way _session_state_path does, rm -f, print nothing, exit 0 on every path. Exit 0 matters twice over here — a ConfigChange hook that exits 2 blocks the config change from taking effect.

Also add a README section covering both status line hooks (the existing SessionStart memo one and this one), and wire the hook into ~/git/macsetup/claude/mbp2022/settings.json and ~/git/macsetup/claude/sbnorge/settings.json.
acceptance:
- bin/clear-statusline-cache.sh deletes the fast cache file for the session id on stdin and leaves the .memo.json file in place.
- It exits 0 and prints nothing for missing stdin, malformed JSON, an absent session_id and a missing file.
- A test under tests/ asserts the filename the script builds equals statusline._fast_cache_path(sid).name, as tests/test_statusline.py:778 does for the memo script.
- README documents both hooks with the settings.json block to paste.
- Both macsetup settings.json files carry the ConfigChange hook.
- just lint-all and just test pass.

CI/CD: gate master, publish the server image on a tag
description:
The repo has no .github/ at all. Every lint and test run is local, and the server image exists only as ccreport:dev, built by `just docker-up` on whichever machine runs it.

Two release tracks on different clocks:

1. The server is a deployed service and wants a named, reproducible artifact — a multi-arch image on GHCR, built for a `server-v*` tag.
2. The CLI and status line are a checkout. `src/ccreport/update_check.py` measures 'an update' in commits past origin/master and `ccreport update --pull` fast-forwards it. That model does not change; the CLI track gets a test gate and nothing else.

Decisions already taken with the user:
- Image is built for a `server-v*` tag only. No `:edge` build on master pushes.
- The sea deployment keeps its branch-based infra playbook. `.deploy.remote.settings.toml` and $INFRA_DIR are out of scope — nothing outside this repo is touched.
- The CLI keeps master-as-release. No tags, no PyPI, no homebrew formula.

Reference material: /Users/ove/git/dogcat/.github/ (uv + just + SHA-pinned actions, dependabot) and https://github.com/kluzzebass/gastrolog/ (.github/workflows/publish.yml — QEMU + buildx + GHCR multi-arch).

Full plan: /Users/ove/.claude/plans/parsed-doodling-treehouse.md

description:
No GitHub Actions run today, so a pull request lands with no lint or test signal. Add the gate that both release tracks share.

Files to create:
- `.github/workflows/ci.yml`
- `.github/dependabot.yml`

ci.yml shape, modelled on /Users/ove/git/dogcat/.github/workflows/ci.yml:
- Triggers: `push: branches: [master]` and `pull_request: branches: [master]`. Note master, not main — dogcat's uses main.
- `concurrency: group: ci-${{ github.ref }}`, `cancel-in-progress: true`.
- One ubuntu-latest job: actions/checkout, astral-sh/setup-uv, `uv python install 3.13`, `uv sync --group dev`, `uvx --from rust-just just lint-all`, `uv run pytest --timeout 30 -n 8 tests`.

Python 3.13 only, no matrix: pyproject.toml sets requires-python = '>=3.13' and ruff target-version = 'py313'.

Do NOT copy dogcat's pnpm and `pnpm install` steps. This repo has no package.json and `just lint-all` is ruff plus pyright, nothing else.

dependabot.yml: the github-actions ecosystem, weekly, all patterns in one group — a straight copy of dogcat's.

Deliberately skipped: dogcat's validate-issues.yml. It runs `uv run dcat doctor`, and dcat is not in this repo's uv.lock.

Split the Dockerfile CMD from docker-compose's dev command
description:
The Dockerfile's CMD is development-shaped and cannot be published as-is. It ends in:

    CMD ["python", "-m", "ccreport.server.fastapi_server", "--host", "0.0.0.0", "--reload"]

`--reload` starts a watchfiles reloader over a bind mount a published image does not have (src/ccreport/server/fastapi_server.py:33). It also silently forces workers to 1 (same file, line 33: `workers=1 if args.reload else args.workers`), which is what one SQLite file wants — so today the correct worker count is an accident of the reload flag.

Changes:
1. `Dockerfile`: CMD becomes `["python", "-m", "ccreport.server.fastapi_server", "--host", "0.0.0.0", "--workers", "1"]`. --workers 1 is explicit because the argparse default is 2 (fastapi_server.py:48).
2. `docker-compose.yml`: add a `command:` on the ccreport-server service carrying the --reload form, so `just docker-up` keeps the behaviour its own comments describe and the read-only ./src mount stays useful.
3. `tests/test_docker_image.py`: new test in the spirit of tests/test_dashboard.py's remote-origin guard. Parse both files and assert the image CMD carries --workers 1 and no --reload, and the compose command carries --reload. They are a pair; an edit to one alone either ships a reloading server or breaks local development with no failing test.

This blocks the release workflow — a tag must not publish a reloading image.
acceptance: `just docker-up` still reloads the container on an edit under src/. `docker build -t ccreport:prod .` then `docker run --rm -p 8788:8787 -e CCREPORT_SERVER_NETWORKS='0.0.0.0/0' ccreport:prod` answers on curl and logs one worker with no reloader. tests/test_docker_image.py passes.

- `permissions: contents: write, packages: write`.
- Two jobs. A `test` job repeating the CI steps (uv sync --group dev, just lint-all, pytest), and an `image` job with `needs: test`, so a tag cannot ship an untested tree.

Quota guard hook: stop the session before extra usage
description:
A quota guard that stops a session before it crosses into extra usage, so an
org account never pays for overflow it did not choose.

Armed by environment only: `CCQUOTA_STOP` unset makes both hooks exit 0 before
they touch Python, so an unarmed session pays one bash spawn per prompt.
`CCQUOTA_WARN=85 CCQUOTA_STOP=95 claude` arms one session; the environment is
read at launch, so a launcher alias is how it gets used in practice.

Hook input carries no quota data — only session_id, transcript_path, cwd,
permission_mode, hook_event_name and effort. The readings come from the local
cache instead: the statusline writes `five_hour` and `seven_day` to
rate_limit_snapshots from Claude Code's own stdin on every render, and the
usage row holds sonnet_percent and scoped_percent from the 10-minute API fetch.

Two hooks, one shared verdict module:

- UserPromptSubmit: over the warn line emits systemMessage; over the stop line
  emits `{"continue": false, "stopReason": ...}`, which halts processing and
  leaves the session open for input.
- PreToolUse: same verdict, so a turn already running halts at its next tool
  call rather than burning to the end of the window.

No hook can exit the CLI. `continue: false` is the strongest stop the harness
offers, and stopReason reaches the person, never Claude.

Fail-closed on an unknown reading, with two distinctions that decide whether
the guard is usable:

- A quota the API nulls because the plan does not have it (see the
  _API_QUOTA_FIELDS comment in usage_api.py) is not applicable, not unknown.
  Conflating them blocks the first prompt of every plan without a Sonnet cap.
- Unknown carries an age. The fetch TTL is 600s, so a reading younger than ~15
  minutes counts and anything older or absent blocks. Say so in the stopReason:
  the way out is unsetting the variable and restarting.

Warnings dedupe on the window instance. Key a TMPDIR memo on resets_at, the
same shape bin/clear-statusline-memo.sh already uses, so one warning lands per
window and a fresh one lands after the window rolls.

Scope note: the quota is per account, not per session. This stops the sessions
that carry the variable on this machine, and nothing else.
acceptance:
- With CCQUOTA_STOP unset, both hooks exit 0 without starting Python.
- Over CCQUOTA_STOP on any watched window, UserPromptSubmit emits continue:
  false and the prompt does not reach the model.
- Over CCQUOTA_STOP mid-turn, PreToolUse halts the next tool call.
- Between CCQUOTA_WARN and CCQUOTA_STOP, one systemMessage lands per window
  instance, not per prompt.
- A quota the API omits or nulls for the plan does not block.
- A reading older than the staleness budget, or no reading at all, blocks, and
  the stopReason names the environment variable to unset.
- Tests cover each verdict against the existing SQLite fixtures.

Split the Dockerfile CMD from docker-compose's dev command
description:
The Dockerfile's CMD is development-shaped and cannot be published as-is. It ends in:

    CMD ["python", "-m", "ccreport.server.fastapi_server", "--host", "0.0.0.0", "--reload"]

`--reload` starts a watchfiles reloader over a bind mount a published image does not have. In src/ccreport/server/fastapi_server.py it also forces one worker, through `workers=1 if args.reload else args.workers` — which is what one SQLite file wants, so today the correct worker count is an accident of the reload flag.

Changes:
1. `Dockerfile`: CMD becomes `["python", "-m", "ccreport.server.fastapi_server", "--host", "0.0.0.0", "--workers", "1"]`. --workers 1 is explicit because argparse defaults it to 2 in the same file.
2. `Dockerfile`: the comment block above that CMD explains that --reload drops the server to one worker. That behaviour moves to docker-compose.yml, so rewrite the comment with the CMD — left alone it describes a flag the line below it no longer carries.
3. `docker-compose.yml`: add a `command:` on the ccreport-server service carrying the --reload form, so `just docker-up` keeps the behaviour its own comments describe and the read-only ./src mount stays useful.
4. `tests/test_docker_image.py`: new test in the spirit of tests/test_dashboard.py's remote-origin guard. Parse both files and assert the image CMD carries --workers 1 and no --reload, and the compose command carries --reload. They are a pair; an edit to one alone either ships a reloading server or breaks local development with no failing test.

This blocks the release workflow — a tag must not publish a reloading image.
acceptance: `just docker-up` still reloads the container on an edit under src/. `docker build -t ccreport:prod .` then `docker run --rm -p 8788:8787 -e CCREPORT_SERVER_NETWORKS='0.0.0.0/0' ccreport:prod` answers on curl and logs one worker with no reloader. tests/test_docker_image.py passes.

Generate synthetic session logs for the JSONL reader
description:
No test parses a Claude Code session log. The suite seeds cache.db directly with fabricated file paths (tests/test_cache_db.py, tests/report_fixture.py), and test_forecast.py keeps its subject off the real ~/.claude/projects. `parse_jsonl_file` in src/ccreport/ccreport.py is the front of the whole pipeline and has no end-to-end coverage, so nobody knows whether `just test` passes on a machine that has never run Claude Code. A GitHub runner is exactly that machine, which is why this blocks ccreport-25in: a red first CI run would not say whether the workflow or the suite is wrong.

Add `tools/make_synthetic_logs.py`, alongside the existing tools/ scripts:

- Takes an output directory and writes a projects/ tree of JSONL session logs into it — several projects, several sessions each, more than one model, and enough days for a report to have rows to group.
- Derive the record shape from `parse_jsonl_file` and the JSONL fields it actually reads, not from memory of Claude Code's format. A generator that writes fields the reader ignores proves nothing.
- Runnable by hand for reproducing a parse bug outside pytest, and importable so a test can build a corpus into tmp_path.
- Nothing is committed as data. The corpus is generated per run; only the script lives in the repo.

Then at least one test that points the reader at a generated tree and asserts what comes back: token counts, model, session and project per record.
acceptance: `python tools/make_synthetic_logs.py <dir>` writes a tree that parse_jsonl_file reads into records. A test builds a corpus into tmp_path and asserts the parsed records match what the generator wrote. `just test` passes with HOME pointed at an empty directory, which is the state a CI runner starts in. No generated JSONL is committed.

Quota guard hook: stop the session before extra usage
description:
A quota guard that stops a session before it crosses into extra usage, so an
org account never pays for overflow it did not choose.

Armed by environment only: `CCQUOTA_STOP` unset makes both hooks exit 0 before
they touch Python, so an unarmed session pays one bash spawn per prompt.
`CCQUOTA_WARN=85 CCQUOTA_STOP=95 claude` arms one session; the environment is
read at launch, so a launcher alias is how it gets used in practice.

Hook input carries no quota data — only session_id, transcript_path, cwd,
permission_mode, hook_event_name and effort. The readings come from the local
cache instead: the statusline writes `five_hour` and `seven_day` to
rate_limit_snapshots from Claude Code's own stdin on every render, and the
usage row holds sonnet_percent and scoped_percent from the 10-minute API fetch.

Two hooks, one shared verdict module:

- UserPromptSubmit: over the warn line emits systemMessage; over the stop line
  emits `{"continue": false, "stopReason": ...}`, which halts processing and
  leaves the session open for input.
- PreToolUse: same verdict, so a turn already running halts at its next tool
  call rather than burning to the end of the window.

No hook can exit the CLI. `continue: false` is the strongest stop the harness
offers, and stopReason reaches the person, never Claude.

Fail-closed on an unknown reading, with two distinctions that decide whether
the guard is usable:

- A quota the API nulls because the plan does not have it (see the
  _API_QUOTA_FIELDS comment in usage_api.py) is not applicable, not unknown.
  Conflating them blocks the first prompt of every plan without a Sonnet cap.
- Unknown carries an age. The fetch TTL is 600s, so a reading younger than ~15
  minutes counts and anything older or absent blocks. Say so in the stopReason:
  the way out is unsetting the variable and restarting.

Warnings dedupe on the window instance. Key a TMPDIR memo on resets_at, the
same shape bin/clear-statusline-memo.sh already uses, so one warning lands per
window and a fresh one lands after the window rolls.

Scope note: the quota is per account, not per session. This stops the sessions
that carry the variable on this machine, and nothing else.
acceptance:
- With CCQUOTA_STOP unset, both hooks exit 0 without starting Python.
- Over CCQUOTA_STOP on any watched window, UserPromptSubmit emits continue:
  false and the prompt does not reach the model.
- Over CCQUOTA_STOP mid-turn, PreToolUse halts the next tool call.
- Between CCQUOTA_WARN and CCQUOTA_STOP, one systemMessage lands per window
  instance, not per prompt.
- A quota the API omits or nulls for the plan does not block.
- A reading older than the staleness budget, or no reading at all, blocks, and
  the stopReason names the environment variable to unset.
- Tests cover each verdict against the existing SQLite fixtures.

Add the CI workflow and dependabot
description:
No GitHub Actions run today, so a pull request lands with no lint or test signal. Add the gate that both release tracks share.

Files to create:
- `.github/workflows/ci.yml`
- `.github/dependabot.yml`

ci.yml shape, modelled on /Users/ove/git/dogcat/.github/workflows/ci.yml:
- Triggers: `push: branches: [master]` and `pull_request: branches: [master]`. Note master, not main — dogcat's uses main.
- `concurrency: group: ci-${{ github.ref }}`, `cancel-in-progress: true`.
- One ubuntu-latest job: actions/checkout, astral-sh/setup-uv, `uv python install 3.13`, `uv sync --group dev --frozen`, `uvx --from rust-just just lint-all`, `uv run pytest --timeout 30 -n 8 tests`.
- Pin every action by commit SHA with a trailing version comment. Reuse the SHAs dogcat already carries.

`--frozen` on the sync is deliberate and differs from dogcat: the Dockerfile already builds that way, and without it a uv.lock that has drifted from pyproject.toml resolves silently, so CI tests a version set no one has run.

Pin pyright too. `just lint-pyright` runs `PYRIGHT_PYTHON_FORCE_VERSION=latest uv run pyright`, which downloads whatever pyright shipped most recently — a release upstream turns master red with no change here. uv.lock resolves pyright 1.1.411; CI should type-check against that. The recipe assigns the variable inline, so a workflow-level `env:` does not win: either make the recipe fall back (`${PYRIGHT_PYTHON_FORCE_VERSION:-latest}`) or have ci.yml run ruff and pyright as their own steps instead of `just lint-all`. Pick one and say which in the pull request.

Python 3.13 only, no matrix: pyproject.toml sets requires-python = '>=3.13' and ruff target-version = 'py313'.

Do NOT copy dogcat's pnpm and `pnpm install` steps. This repo has no package.json and `just lint-all` is ruff plus pyright, nothing else. Its `fetch-depth: 0` is also unnecessary: every git call in the suite is a stubbed subprocess.run (tests/test_update_check.py, tests/test_update_command.py), so a shallow checkout tests the same thing.

dependabot.yml: the github-actions ecosystem, weekly, all patterns in one group — a straight copy of dogcat's.

Deliberately skipped: dogcat's validate-issues.yml. It runs `uv run dcat doctor`, and dcat is not in this repo's uv.lock.
acceptance: The pull request that adds these files shows a green CI check on GitHub. `just lint-all` and `just test` pass locally against the same tree.

title: Quota guard hook: stop the session before extra usage
Quota guard hook: stop the session before extra usage
description:
A quota guard that stops a session before it crosses into extra usage, so an
org account never pays for overflow it did not choose.

Armed by environment only: `CCQUOTA_STOP` unset makes both hooks exit 0 before
they touch Python, so an unarmed session pays one bash spawn per prompt.
`CCQUOTA_WARN=85 CCQUOTA_STOP=95 claude` arms one session; the environment is
read at launch, so a launcher alias is how it gets used in practice.

Hook input carries no quota data — only session_id, transcript_path, cwd,
permission_mode, hook_event_name and effort. The readings come from the local
cache instead: the statusline writes `five_hour` and `seven_day` to
rate_limit_snapshots from Claude Code's own stdin on every render, and the
usage row holds sonnet_percent and scoped_percent from the 10-minute API fetch.

Two hooks, one shared verdict module:

- UserPromptSubmit: over the warn line emits systemMessage; over the stop line
  emits `{"continue": false, "stopReason": ...}`, which halts processing and
  leaves the session open for input.
- PreToolUse: same verdict, so a turn already running halts at its next tool
  call rather than burning to the end of the window.

No hook can exit the CLI. `continue: false` is the strongest stop the harness
offers, and stopReason reaches the person, never Claude.

Fail-closed on an unknown reading, with two distinctions that decide whether
the guard is usable:

- A quota the API nulls because the plan does not have it (see the
  _API_QUOTA_FIELDS comment in usage_api.py) is not applicable, not unknown.
  Conflating them blocks the first prompt of every plan without a Sonnet cap.
- Unknown carries an age. The fetch TTL is 600s, so a reading younger than ~15
  minutes counts and anything older or absent blocks. Say so in the stopReason:
  the way out is unsetting the variable and restarting.

Warnings dedupe on the window instance. Key a TMPDIR memo on resets_at, the
same shape bin/clear-statusline-memo.sh already uses, so one warning lands per
window and a fresh one lands after the window rolls.

Scope note: the quota is per account, not per session. This stops the sessions
that carry the variable on this machine, and nothing else.
acceptance:
- With CCQUOTA_STOP unset, both hooks exit 0 without starting Python.
- Over CCQUOTA_STOP on any watched window, UserPromptSubmit emits continue:
  false and the prompt does not reach the model.
- Over CCQUOTA_STOP mid-turn, PreToolUse halts the next tool call.
- Between CCQUOTA_WARN and CCQUOTA_STOP, one systemMessage lands per window
  instance, not per prompt.
- A quota the API omits or nulls for the plan does not block.
- A reading older than the staleness budget, or no reading at all, blocks, and
  the stopReason names the environment variable to unset.
- Tests cover each verdict against the existing SQLite fixtures.
